preamble: The shift from the voiceless bilabial fricative [ɸ] to the voiceless glottal fricative [h] is a debuccalization: the labial constriction is lost and friction remains only at the glottis. The textbook case is Japanese, where Old Japanese *p became [ɸ] in Middle Japanese (written ⟨f⟩ in Portuguese missionary works and ⟨ph⟩/⟨hw⟩ in the Korean textbook Ch'ŏphae Sinŏ) and then [h] in Early Modern Japanese, except before /u/, where [ɸ] survives. A bilabial [ɸ] stage is widely reconstructed (though not directly attested) for the Old Castilian change of Latin f- to h-. Because [ɸ] is itself a cross-linguistically uncommon phoneme, the change is attested in only a handful of well-described cases; commonality is set to 3.

examples.note: 'mother'; the attested chain is /papa/ > /ɸaɸa/ > /ɸawa/ > /ɸaɸa/ > /haha/ (Wiktionary, citing Nihon Kokugo Daijiten)
The shift to [h] did not apply before /u/, so modern /h/ is still realized [ɸ] in that position

examples.from: Latin facere 'to do' > Old Spanish fazer
examples.note: Reconstructed chain [f] > [ɸ] > [h] > ∅ (Penny); the [ɸ] stage is inferred, not directly attested
Initial [h] from Latin f- survives in rural western dialects (e.g. Extremadura, western Andalusia).

sources: Frellesvig, B. (2010). A History of the Japanese Language. https://doi.org/10.1017/CBO9780511778322
Penny, R. (2002). A History of the Spanish Language. https://doi.org/10.1017/cbo9780511992827
